verdict: GEOGRAPHIC PASS · PRIMARY HIKE PASS · SCRAMBLE AND TRAIL ART CONDITIONAL. Not full acceptance.
summary: B2a fixes the four B1.1 geographic defects in the geometry, without loosening any criterion. No seam cluster exceeds 0.25 ha (B1.1 had four). The Western Col is at 681.4 m and gives Vesttind 54.4 m of prominence (B1.1: 695.3 m and 40.5 m). The dry hollow drains through a natural outlet. Coast, water, High Tarn, corridors and every other route are byte-identical.

B1.1's character survives in every identity view. The summit is unchanged at 897.04 m and is still the island maximum. The three arms, the cirques, the asymmetric crown and the Birchwood and Central Valley silhouettes all read the same. Outside the two declared windows the skyline moves at most 0.51 px.
The primary hiking approach is comfortable on the terrain: 3.0 km to the Vestfjell shoulder viewpoint, no metre above 0.30, max 0.296, no cross-slope above 0.5.

The optional scramble is not acceptable yet. It runs 8 m above its own 0.50 limit, 69 % of it has cross-slope above 0.5, and it has no usable tread. It is longer and steeper than the B1.1 summit section, and it first drops 66 m below the viewpoint. The heightfield bench also produces visible artefacts: a sawtooth on the north arête skyline and thin hard chevrons at the hairpins. Both need dedicated trail geometry, not more heightfield editing.

questions: Yes. In Birchwood and the Central Valley the B1.1 and B2a frames are hard to tell apart. The crown, the dominant summit and the three-arm massing are unchanged. The west-arm end is slightly lower and softer, the declared D1 change.
Do the coastal ends look natural now?

Clearly better. The north-west arm and the Vesttind buttress now run down to the sea instead of ending in a stepped sea cliff. The isolated lit fin at the north headland is gone, and the hard crease band beside the windward gully is replaced by a continuous flank.
Does the Western Col read as a col?
Yes. From the south and from the viewpoint, Vesttind now stands as its own top over a real saddle, instead of merging into the North Peak shoulder.
Yes, as a small descending notch. The first carve had a comb of notches, which was fixed. In an aerial view the outlet is barely noticeable, which is right for its size.
How do the route and benches read?

The primary benches are mostly subtle. At hairpins and on traverses they show as thin, hard, perfectly straight scratches, which reads engineered. On the scramble the bench breaks the north arête into a sawtooth that is visible on the skyline from the route. That is a defect.

A better landform than B1.1 with the same identity. The remaining problems are trail geometry, not terrain. They belong in a dedicated trail mesh (ribbon plus collision), not in further heightfield edits.

defects.title: Optional scramble exceeds its own 0.50 limit (8 m, max 0.516). 69 % of it has cross-slope above 0.5 and it has no usable tread. It is longer (1223 m) and steeper than the B1.1 summit section (246 m, max 0.475). It first descends 66 m from the viewpoint (708.6 → 642.4 m) across the south face before climbing, so the summit costs 267 m of ascent for 188 m of net gain.

limitations: Captures are SwiftShader renders in clay material only. No vegetation, texture or trail ribbon is shown.
The tread is measured on the 4 m heightfield; a 1–2 m tread is only approximated.
The viewer walk rule (grade ≤ 0.7) proves walkability, not comfort; comfort is the hiking-grade and cross-slope metrics.
Walk cameras stand on whichever terrain is loaded, so the B1.1 frame at a B2a route camera is not on a B1.1 route.
Art judgement is one reviewer's reading of the captures.
